rv.q: New Yorkers and visitors to this city currently have a chance to witness the transcendence of a musical theater masterpiece.
Into the Woods is a blissful contradiction: musical fantasy that puts us back in touch with reality.
The scintillating new revival of “Into the Woods” is rendered so harmoniously and meticulously, you’ll swear you even hear the punctuation marks in the lyrics.

It's a crystalline showcase for sensational performances from an all-star cast of marquee veterans, and a testament to the enduring genius of the beloved musical, now in its fourth Broadway incarnation since premiering in 1987.
When even an understudy playing a cow manages to delight, you know a show has hit all its marks, and then some.

That’s the case with Lear deBessonet’s gorgeous production, which began as a semi-staged concert in the Encores! series this spring and now moves to Broadway for a limited 8-week run, with a mix of superlative original cast and sparkling new additions.
Lear deBessonet's superb production of the Sondheim and James Lapine modern classic 'Into the Woods'... its humor, wonder and humanity have arrived intact.

It is successful not unlike the way the long-running revival of “Chicago” became successful, by cutting away what it did not need and allowing for an atypical intense, direct communication with the audience.
Even when the giant starts stomping around and the cast goes boom-squish, you still find reasons to laugh. It's a tonic.
Into the Woods's legion fans are well-served by this revival, and at both the Encores! performance and the Broadway press performance that I attended, the audience response was overwhelming.
Maybe it was just that hard-to-describe thing that happens when every piston fires on time, every gear meshes, every valve syncs up, and the thing really takes off down the road.
Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine's mythical musical remains a delight.
Surely Into the Woods Is one of them.
This Red is a multi-dimensional creation, much like this perfect production.
This is a theatrical event to see and to savor.

In striping Woods down to its bare essentials, the very brilliant DeBessonet has crafted a near-perfect revival that breathes intoxicating new life into a masterpiece we barely realized needed new life at all.
And in this production, it feels revelatory once again.
They say three's a charm — and this revival has it to spare.

Now that it's officially on its feet at the St. James Theatre, I would like to submit Into the Woods as proof to this skeptical industry that there is a not-so-far-off kingdom where the pinnacle of art meets the pinnacle of entertainment.
The current Broadway production staged by Lear deBessonet may be the most definitive of them all.

This Into the Woods revival is eminently worth seeing, for perhaps an unusual additional reason. When I attended, the audience cheered every first-act song long and loud. Why such jubilation? If the timing of this production enhances its enchantment, the appeal is undeniable.
This principle of “less is more”, allowed me to take in the meat of Into the Woods like never before.
“Into The Woods” is a spectacular dose of joy.
This revival of Into the Woods is a stripped-down, intimate production that allows the brilliant score and lyrics to shine while maintaining the emotional complexity of Sondheim's masterpiece.
The show is simply and ingeniously staged, with an onstage orchestra and a stand of trees as the main scenery.
Lear deBessonet’s stripped-down, elegantly simplified staging, which focuses on the score and performances rather than elaborate visuals, is thoroughly enjoyable.

cn.t: Critics hail this stripped-down revival as a transcendent tribute to Sondheim, with the pared-back staging allowing the brilliant score and emotional complexity to shine through a starry, impeccably performed cast.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at St. James Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,710 seats, St. James Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.
